article_title: Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math
citation: Catherine Nelson, Julia Kaufman, Kevin Booker, Brian Gill. (2007). Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. Cambridge, MA: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/elementary-grade-math-programs-in-the-pittsburgh-public-schools-a-comparison-of-everyday-mathematics-and-harcourt-math
title: Evaluate curriculum programs as implemented, since implementation similarity can mask theoretical differences between programs
description: When comparing curricula, program effects depend on how programs are actually enacted in classrooms, not only on their theoretical design. The Pittsburgh comparison found no achievement difference between Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, and the authors suggest this "may be related to the fact that" the programs "were more similar in practice than they are in theory." Evaluations should therefore attend to implementation when interpreting program comparisons.
requirements: Assessment of how the programs were actually implemented in classrooms, so that implementation similarity can be taken into account when interpreting outcome differences.
constraints: The article states this interpretation only for the Pittsburgh implementation of these two programs; it is offered as a possible explanation, not a tested finding.
target_learners: Elementary-grade students in public school districts
target_learning_goals: Elementary mathematics achievement
examples: The Pittsburgh quasi-experimental comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math, in which the authors attributed the null achievement difference to the programs' similar implementation in practice.

Elementary-Grade Math Programs in the Pittsburgh Public Schools: A Comparison of Everyday Mathematics and Harcourt Math. title: Adult education programs should use evidence-based strategies to improve services and participant success
description: The report states that "WIOA encourages adult education programs to use evidence-based strategies to improve services and participant success." constraints: The report finds there is not yet much evidence available to guide such decision making

high school equivalency

article_title: Improvements in Math Instruction and Student Achievement Through Professional Learning Around the Common Core State Standards in Chicago
citation: Key Questions: How did students' reports of instructional practices, their test scores, grades, and pass rates in math change with implementation of the CCSS-M, based on their schools' level of participation in standards-related PL?. (2018). AERA Open. https://aeraopen.org
title: Evaluate standards implementation by implementation strategy, student subgroups, and outcomes beyond test scores
description: The article argues that existing literature on the Common Core State Standards in Math showed little benefit but had not examined variation by implementation strategies, student subgroups, or outcomes other than test scores. It therefore designs its evaluation around "different levels of participation in professional learning around the standards," subgroup achievement levels, and grades, pass rates, and practice reports. This broadens what counts as evidence of a standards policy's effects.
requirements: Outcome data beyond test scores, such as student reports of instructional practices, grades, and pass rates, must be available
constraints: Findings are from one district (Chicago) and the middle grades, so generalization to other settings is not established in the available text
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement under standards-based reform
examples: The study compared pre- and post-standards years across Chicago middle-grade schools with different levels of professional-learning participation using a difference-in-differences approach with school fixed effects.

article_title: Want to Improve Teaching? Create Collaborative, Supportive Schools
citation: Elaine Allensworth. (2012). Want to Improve Teaching? Create Collaborative, Supportive Schools. American Educator, Fall 2012. http://www.annenberginstitute.org/VUE
title: Base teacher evaluation and performance policy on school context, not individual teachers alone
description: The article argues that strategies assuming instructional quality is inherent in the teacher fail because teachers face very different working conditions; evaluation systems that "judge teachers without regard to context can further disincentivize teaching in the hardest environments." It recommends using instruction and performance data to drive conversations about practice and build professional community, and prioritizing development of collaborative relationships among teachers, leaders, and families over identifying a few effective or ineffective individuals.
requirements: Systems that support teachers around instruction, including collaboration that provides insight into better practice
constraints: Value-added and observation-based evaluation protocols commonly make no adjustments for the types of students being served; context-blind incentives risk increasing turnover in unstable schools
target_learners: Students in urban and disadvantaged schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained instructional improvement and equitable educational outcomes
examples: The article describes how data on classroom instruction and student performance can structure professional development and build a school's professional community focused on instruction and learning occurring in the building

article_title: Changing Special Education Enrollments
citation: Shazia Rafiullah Miller and Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Changing Special Education Enrollments: Causes and Distribution Among Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Consider elementary school policies in light of their possible long-term effects on high schools before adopting them
description: This principle holds that district policymakers should project the downstream consequences of elementary school reforms for high schools before adoption. The report's central finding is that the eighth-grade promotion gate, an elementary policy, reshaped high school composition by retaining general education students while students with disabilities advanced under IEP requirements, concentrating them in neighborhood schools. As the report puts it, "before the system adopts a policy to prompt change in the elementary schools, it should be considered in light of its possible long-term effects on high schools."
requirements: Requires longitudinal enrollment and classification data spanning grade levels so cross-level effects can be projected before adoption
constraints: The report grounds this in one district (Chicago, 1993–2000) and one policy (the 1995–96 eighth-grade promotion gate) with its specific retention, APC, and IEP rules
target_learners: eighth-grade students transitioning to high school
students with disabilities in neighborhood high schools
target_learning_goals: equitable distribution of students with disabilities across schools
inclusion of students with disabilities in general education classrooms
system-level policy design that anticipates cross-level consequences
examples: The report traces how the 1995–96 eighth-grade promotion gate produced higher general education retention, a smaller better-prepared ninth-grade cohort, and concentrations of students with disabilities reaching 30 percent in eleven high schools
key_sources: Shazia Rafiullah Miller and Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Changing Special Education Enrollments: Causes and Distribution Among Schools. article_title: Students improve even amid evaluation controversy
citation: NWEA Research. (2016). Students improve even amid evaluation controversy. Phi Delta Kappan 98 (2), 58-65. https://www.nwea.org
title: Strengthen evaluation procedures, systematic evidence collection, and data use rather than relying on a punitive approach
description: The article recommends improving the teacher evaluation process by emphasizing "the importance of strong evaluation procedures, the systematic collection of evidence of teacher performance, and the use of data to inform the process." target_learning_goals: Improving educator effectiveness and student achievement over time
examples: New York's APPR system combined a student-growth component (40%) with classroom observations (60%) as an instance of structured, evidence-based evaluation

citation: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275

article_title: The Unknown World of Charter High Schools
citation: Kevin Booker, Tim R. Sass, Brian Gill, Ron Zimmer. (2010). The Unknown World of Charter High Schools. Education Next, vol. 10, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Evaluate charter high schools on attainment outcomes such as diploma completion and college attendance, not test scores alone
description: The article argues that attainment outcomes should anchor evaluations of charter high schools because of their downstream stakes: "Given the impact of educational attainment on a variety of economic and social outcomes, a positive result could have significant implications for the value of school-choice programs that include charter high schools." The study therefore measures standard diploma receipt and college attendance rather than relying solely on achievement tests.

constraints: The recommendation is grounded in the authors' framing of attainment's economic and social importance, not in a tested comparison of evaluation methods

target_learning_goals: high school completion
college attendance
examples: The study measured the likelihood of earning a standard diploma and of attending college as its primary outcomes for charter high school attendees in Chicago and Florida

citation: Hale, S., Dunn, L., Filby, N., Rice, J., & Van Houten, L. (2017). title: Five-step continuous improvement framework for evidence-based school and district improvement
description: The guide presents a five-part continuous improvement framework that brings together two ideas: that decisions should be based on data and evidence, and that "a continuous improvement process is fundamental to engaging in and sustaining improvements in school and district practice." article_title: AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice
citation: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417
title: Evidence-present versus evidence-effectively-available distinction for AI assessment of documents
description: The article proposes a methodological distinction for AI-based assessment: evidence contained in a student report is not the same as evidence the model can actually retrieve during processing. As the article states, "the fact that evidence is present in a report does not necessarily mean that such evidence is effectively available to the model during processing." An equation may be in the document yet inadequately retrieved, and a graph may be uninterpretable if axes, units, or legends are not legible. This distinction explains why model-instructor differences may reflect document processing rather than physics reasoning, and it conditions the information on which the model operates.
requirements: Assessment with AI requires attention to how reports are processed and what information can actually be retrieved, not only to model capabilities.
constraints: The article notes OCR systems and multimodal models still show limitations with visually complex documents, and high character-recognition accuracy does not guarantee preservation of document structure and meaning.
target_learners: higher education students in experimental physics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment and feedback on laboratory reports
examples: The article notes a graph may contain relevant information that cannot be interpreted if its axes, units, or legends are not legible during processing.

article_title: AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics
citation: Markus S. Feser & Paul L. Tschisgale. (2026). AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics. Physics Education, Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education, Kiel. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8503-0951
title: Evaluate AI-based scoring not only by agreement with expert ratings but also by whether disagreements rest on construct-irrelevant information
description: The article argues that agreement with expert ratings is necessary but not sufficient for valid AI-based scoring: an AI can reproduce expert scores well while its deviations remain systematically tied to construct-irrelevant features such as linguistic quality. Evaluations should therefore examine, in the article's words, "to what extent disagreements rest on construct -irrelevant information", for example by modelling whether scoring deviations are associated with linguistic quality as this study did.

article_title: ASE-26: A Curriculum for Agentic Software Engineering as a Discipline
citation: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline.
title: The evolutionary spiral: co-evolution of intent and build across agent-mediated turns
description: The evolutionary spiral is the article's central conceptual contribution: a project runs as a sequence of turns in which work inside a turn is fast and loose while between turns intent is pinned down, the specification is updated and the context file absorbs what was learned. It synthesises Boehm's risk-driven spiral model, the design-research account of co-evolution of problem and solution spaces, and Brooks's contracting-point refinement of iterative process. The article states that "Across many turns the project converges on a definite version of what was actually wanted, even though no single turn could have known the final destination." It is taught in Module 18 and operationalised through two judgment skills, the commit point and drift detection.
requirements: Practitioners must learn commit-point and drift-detection judgment skills, which the article says are learned through practice rather than instruction
constraints: The article notes the two judgment skills cannot be taught the way verification gate design can; a companion pre-print will develop the contrast with spec-driven approaches at full length
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students with foundational computer science knowledge
target_learning_goals: managing iterative human-agent software projects
discovering requirements through build-evaluate-revise cycles
examples: A semester project that takes a small software product across at least three full turns of the evolutionary spiral, graded on mid-project commit-point decisions and recoveries from drift
key_sources: Mikael Gorsky (Holon Institute of Technology). (2026). ASE-26: a curriculum for agentic software engineering as a discipline. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01152

article_title: EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation
citation: Geonwoo Bang, Dongho Kim, and Moohong Min. (2026). EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation. arXiv:2610.03273. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03273
title: EVOL: simulator-guided demonstration learning for deployment-free learning path recommendation
description: EVOL adapts the robotics sim-to-real demonstration recipe to educational recommendation: a DKT-based knowledge evolution simulator (KES) both synthesizes per-learner expert paths via evolutionary search and hosts RL fine-tuning, while the deployed actor plans from the initial mastery alone. Per the article, "An asymmetric actor-critic architecture has the actor commit to blind planning from h0 in keeping the inference constraint while the critic exploits the privileged evolving mastery h𝑡 for accurate value targets during training." Training has three stages: evolutionary expert generation, behavioral cloning, and PPO fine-tuning with a warm-started privileged critic. At deployment the actor alone emits the full L-step path with no KES query.
requirements: A trained DKT simulator queryable during training
A combinatorial sequence decision problem with sparse terminal reward
Instance-specific near-optimal sequences that human demonstrations cannot supply
constraints: The deployed policy cannot access the simulator or counterfactual intermediate feedback at inference time
Demonstrations inherit whatever the DKT fails to represent, such as identical dynamics for learners with identical histories regardless of aptitude
target_learners: online learners on tutoring platforms with interaction histories
target_learning_goals: maximizing mastery improvement on target concepts via ordered learning paths
examples: Stage 1 evolves a population of 60 candidate paths over 50 generations inside the KES, selecting the single best path per learner; Stage 2 distills experts via behavioral cloning; Stage 3 refines with asymmetric PPO
key_sources: Geonwoo Bang, Dongho Kim, and Moohong Min. (2026). EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation. arXiv:2610.03273. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03273

article_title: Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms
citation: Csépányi-Fürjes, L., & Kovács, L. (2026). Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms with intuitionistic fuzzy logic and forgetting. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10639-6
title: Evolving Knowledge Space Graph (EKSG) model
description: The EKSG model is a graph-structured knowledge representation framework for adaptive intelligent tutoring in fast-changing domains, combining the structural clarity of ontologies with the adaptive potential of Competence-Based Knowledge Space Theory. The article describes it as "a Knowledge Space Theory (KST) based (Doignon & Falmagne, 1985) conceptual framework specifically designed to support adaptive intelligent tutoring in fast-changing domains" that "integrates principles of temporal graph theory to represent dynamically changing domains." In this study it is operationalized in the G4L system, with knowledge units, material units, and test units as graph nodes connected by prerequisite_of edges.
requirements: A graph database to represent and query the prerequisite structure among knowledge units, as implemented in Neo4j
constraints: Before this study there was no publicly available implementation of the model and no empirical studies evaluating its practical feasibility or pedagogical utility
target_learners: university students in fast-evolving domains such as computer science
target_learning_goals: structured domain knowledge acquisition and adaptive learning pathways in dynamic curricula
examples: Operationalized in the Graph4Learn system for the JDBC API subdomain of a Database Systems II course, segmented into 15 knowledge units
key_sources: Csépányi-Fürjes, L., & Kovács, L. (2026). Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms with intuitionistic fuzzy logic and forgetting. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10639-6

article_title: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning
citation: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161
title: Evidence-grounded multimodal lecture-to-KG pipeline
description: An end-to-end pipeline combining "timestamped automatic speech recognition (ASR), high-recall anchor selection, OCR, grounded vision-language extraction, validation, canonicalization, KG construction, and GraphRAG-style retrieval." Its design constraint is that "a concept or relationship is promoted only when tied to lecture evidence." Unlike slide- or transcript-only educational KG pipelines, it treats video frames, OCR output, and transcript segments as three simultaneous evidence sources for the same anchor, capturing diagram- and equation-only content. The output is a NetworkX MultiDiGraph whose edges carry relation type, lecture, timestamp, anchor, evidence quotation, and confidence.
requirements: Every mention must cite transcript, OCR, or visual evidence before entering the graph; extraction is constrained to a fixed education-oriented relation vocabulary of eight permitted types
constraints: Validation improves auditability but does not by itself guarantee factual correctness; the evaluation covers only three lectures from one series
target_learners: instructors and learners using lecture-video question answering in neural-network coursework
target_learning_goals: answering lecture questions about concepts, prerequisites, and cross-lecture relationships in instructional video
examples: On three 3Blue1Brown lectures the pipeline processed 3,118 frames, 756 transcript segments, and 559 anchors, producing 172 canonical concepts and 282 relationships
key_sources: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161

article_title: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning
citation: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161
title: Evidence-grounding extraction schema for auditable educational knowledge graphs
description: The paper's organizing framework is an extraction schema in which every extracted item retains "evidence, confidence, modality, lecture, timestamp, frame, and anchor identifiers." A concept records name, definition, evidence quotation, source modality, and confidence; a relationship records source, target, one of eight permitted types, evidence quotation, modality, and confidence. The authors argue such auditability matters in education because unsupported claims can mislead learners and instructors need to inspect or correct extracted knowledge. Each retained mention records its full provenance, reducing the risk of a structurally plausible but unsupported VLM-generated graph.
requirements: Transcript- and OCR-sourced claims must occur in the evidence pool; visual-only concepts require stronger confidence; confidence below 0.55 is removed
constraints: The authors state validation improves auditability but does not by itself guarantee factual correctness
target_learners: instructors inspecting or correcting automatically extracted course knowledge
target_learning_goals: trustworthy, traceable lecture question answering over multi-lecture course content
examples: Each edge in the constructed graph records endpoints, type, and supporting evidence, so answers can be traced to a specific transcript span, OCR string, or frame

article_title: Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics
citation: Vy Le, Jayson M. Nissen, Jason W. Morphew, Hua Hua Chang, and Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09584
title: Evidence-centered design as the framework linking MCD learning objectives to observable response evidence
description: The article frames MCD development within evidence-centered design (ECD), in which "the student models specify the knowledge an assessment makes claims about, and the evidence models specify the link between observed responses and those claims." ECD comprises five models (student, evidence, task, assembly, and delivery); this paper focuses on the student models (the 14 LOs) and evidence models (the Q-matrix and DINA model). The authors treat DINA fit and classification accuracy as validity evidence for the student models, testing whether the LOs defined a priori are measurable and separable in student responses.
requirements: Developers with both content and context expertise, evidence-based reasoning to draw inferences, and attention to practical constraints such as available resources and testing conditions
constraints: Weak fit or low classification accuracy indicates limited supporting evidence for a portion of the student models, whether from items, sample, or measurement model
target_learners: College students in introductory mechanics courses
target_learning_goals: Mastery of fine-grained introductory mechanics learning objectives
key_sources: Vy Le, Jayson M. Nissen, Jason W. Morphew, Hua Hua Chang, and Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09584

article_title: A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education
citation: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874
title: Gate AI feedback generation on recorded evidence and escalate assistance progressively with calibrated risk
description: The article recommends that feedback systems let calibrated risk guide intervention timing, constrain feedback content to recorded evidence, and progress assistance from self-checks to localized hints when warranted. Each generated message contains an evidence-based observation, a feasible next action, a learner self-check, and an optional exact code excerpt, and the instruction "prohibited complete solutions and claims not supported by the supplied evidence." Unverifiable references are removed rather than retained.
requirements: A bounded learner record available at the decision moment
Calibrated risk estimates with validation-fitted thresholds
Automated structural and source-verification checks with a repair pass and human review routing
constraints: The article notes that unrestricted generative assistance can improve supported practice while reducing later unassisted performance, motivating guardrails; the progressive-assistance mapping was evaluated on structural and provenance checks, not on learning outcomes
target_learners: introductory programming students in higher education
target_learning_goals: independent debugging and revision behavior
self-regulated monitoring and verification
examples: In the F4 condition, risk-based instructions were assigned to all 136 cases: 31 received the self-check level, 80 the concept-hint level, and 25 the localized-hint level, with all cases below the prespecified ensemble-disagreement threshold.
key_sources: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874

article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: Evaluation-agnostic annotation framework with user-defined dimensions, arbitrary rating scales, and weighted aggregation
description: MuTSE operates as an evaluation-agnostic framework with zero predefined metrics: evaluators build custom assessment criteria from scratch in the Settings module, define arbitrary numerical rating scales from binary (1-to-2) up to continuous 100-point sliders, and assign relative impact weights from 0.1 to 10.0. The system normalizes and aggregates manual inputs to compute a weighted overall performance percentage for each generated column. The article motivates this by noting "a pervasive lack of standardization and extreme diversity in evaluation methodologies and terminology across the field."
requirements: Evaluators must define their own dimensions, scales, and weights through the Settings module before annotation
constraints: The article cites debate over rating scales, noting discrete Likert scales' application frequently deviates from best practices and researchers advocate continuous scales
target_learners: Educators and applied linguists assessing simplified texts
target_learning_goals: Qualitative scoring of simplification quality on dimensions such as fluency and meaning preservation
examples: The interface embeds the exact cosine-similarity alignment score inline with each generated sentence to accelerate detection of unwanted LLM conversational artifacts or unprompted semantic hallucinations

article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Learning Engagement Among Medical Undergraduates: Statistical Indirect and Configurational Associations Involving Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction
citation: He Qian, Chang Guanglei, Su Ning, Yang Yingying, Ma Jun. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Learning Engagement Among Medical Undergraduates: Statistical Indirect and Configurational Associations Involving Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091694
title: Evaluate GAI integration by students' psychological need conditions rather than frequency of use alone
description: The article recommends that educational relevance of GAI use be judged in relation to students' psychological need conditions rather than use frequency alone. It states that "the educational relevance of GAI use may be better understood in relation to students' psychological need conditions than to use frequency alone," and that medical schools "may place less emphasis on the frequency of GAI use alone when integrating GAI into teaching." This follows from the weak direct GAI–engagement association and the core role of competence need satisfaction in the principal configuration.
requirements: Measurement or observation of psychological need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) alongside GAI use
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional associations among medical undergraduates and do not establish causal effects
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: learning engagement
autonomous motivation

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Evaluate setting and learning material before applying interleaving in educational settings
description: Because the interleaving effect's magnitude and even direction depend on the type and characteristics of the learning material, the article concludes that "interleaving can effectively foster inductive learning but that the setting and the type of learning material must be considered." Educators should verify that material resembles the conditions where interleaving works (e.g., visually similar categories) before adopting it, and should "use with caution in certain conditions, especially for expository texts and words."
requirements: Learning material and setting should be evaluated for similarity structure before adopting interleaved sequencing
constraints: Interleaving showed a blocking advantage for word materials and no significant effect for expository texts and tastes
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and classification
examples: The meta-analysis quantified material-type differences, with paintings at g = 0.67 and words at g = -0.39, as the empirical basis for this recommendation.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Evaluation frameworks: structures specifying aspects of implementation that could be evaluated
description: The fifth category, evaluation frameworks, provides "a structure for evaluating implementation endeavours" by specifying aspects of implementation that could be evaluated to determine implementation success. Examples are RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance), PRECEDE-PROCEED, and Proctor et al.'s framework of eight implementation outcomes: acceptability, adoption, appropriateness, costs, feasibility, fidelity, penetration and sustainability. Approaches from the other four categories can also serve evaluation purposes because they specify concepts that may be operationalized and measured.
requirements: Specification of concepts and constructs that may be operationalized and measured
target_learning_goals: evaluating implementation success
examples: Proctor et al.'s framework was developed on the basis of a narrative literature review proposing eight conceptually distinct outcomes
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Event segmentation theory: people mentally segment dynamic visualizations during perception, and instructional segmentation can cue relevant event boundaries
description: Event segmentation theory (Zacks et al. 2007) "describes the processes underlying mental segmentation": people form event models in working memory, predict what happens next, and distinguish an event boundary when predictions and incoming sensory information differ too much. Physical and structural changes decrease predictability and mark boundaries; more extensive processing occurs at boundaries, so more information about them is stored in long-term memory. The review proposes that instructional segmentation works partly by cueing these boundaries — "rather than relying on students' ability to mentally segment the dynamic visualisations, this is done for them" — aiding perception of the underlying structure and chunking.
requirements: Event boundaries in the material should correspond to meaningful subevents or substeps of the depicted process or procedure
constraints: Students with higher levels of prior knowledge might not need these temporal cues or might even be hampered by them, because guidance must be reconciled with their available schemas
target_learners: Students learning from dynamic visualizations of processes and procedures, particularly novices
target_learning_goals: Perceiving the structure underlying a depicted process or procedure; remembering subevents and their temporal order
examples: The review links segmentation to Catrambone's work on labeled, visually isolated calculation substeps, which raised learning outcomes and prompted students to mention substeps in their procedure descriptions

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Evaluative judgement: the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others
description: The paper defines evaluative judgement as "the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others", simplifying an earlier definition by Tai et al. (2016). It has two complementary components: understanding what constitutes quality, and applying that understanding through appraisal of one's own or others' work. The paper positions it as an integrating concept underpinning self-assessment, peer assessment, exemplars and feedback, aimed at preparing students for future learning and practice beyond graduation.
requirements: Development of evaluative judgement must be deliberate and deliberated upon, through repeated engagement with standards and appraisal of work
constraints: Evaluative judgement is contextual and domain specific: what constitutes quality depends on the setting and disciplinary area, though the capability of identifying criteria may cross domains
target_learning_goals: judging quality of own and others' work
lifelong learning and sustainable assessment
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Common design features of evaluative-judgement pedagogies: iterative criteria engagement, judging diverse work samples, and justified dialogue
description: Across the five practices, the paper identifies shared design features: "active and iterative engagement with criteria, the enactment of judgements on diverse samples of work, dialogic feedback with peers and tutors oriented towards understanding quality", and articulation and justification of judgements with a focus on both immediate and future tasks. Evaluative judgement refocuses these activities as pedagogies producing students who can judge effectively within and beyond the course.
requirements: Opportunities at every stage of a course: discussions, task planning and debriefing, assessment and feedback design, and continuing discourse about purpose
constraints: The pattern derives from conceptual analysis of previous work rather than empirical testing; the authors call for empirical studies of the strategies
target_learning_goals: making effective judgements of quality within and beyond the course
examples: The paper positions exemplar use, rubric co-creation, and self and peer assessment and feedback as work-intensive activities justified by this overarching purpose

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Evaluate games for learning through an evidence-based approach using testable questions, appropriate methods, and learning theory
description: The book advocates that claims about the educational effectiveness of games be evaluated scientifically rather than through unsupported claims, popularity, or anecdotes. "An evidence-based approach to the study of games for learning involves using appropriate research methods, grounded in learning theory, to yield data needed for answering testable questions." The approach is self-correcting: as evidence accumulates, unhelpful accounts of learning with games can be rejected and more useful ones constructed. Reports based primarily on selected anecdotes or testimonials do not qualify as evidence-based.
requirements: Research must pose testable questions, use appropriate research methods, and be grounded in theories of learning relevant to games
constraints: Evidence must come from methodologically sound studies; anecdote, popularity, and unsupported assertion do not qualify
target_learners: students and researchers of educational games
target_learning_goals: determining the educational effectiveness of computer games for learning
examples: The book reviews only studies that randomly assign participants, match treatment and control groups, and use appropriate measures of learning outcome
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Evidence-centered assessment design (ECD): competency, evidence, task/action, and assembly models
description: ECD is "a conceptual design framework to help in the creation of coherent assessments" supporting "a broad range of assessment types, from classroom quizzes to simulation-based assessments." The competency model defines knowledge, skills, abilities and other attributes as probability distributions per variable; the evidence model specifies what student actions count as evidence and how it statistically links to competency variables; task/action models express situations that evoke required evidence; and the assembly model specifies how the models work together to form a valid assessment. Statistical machinery such as IRT or Bayesian networks links observable data to unobservable competencies.
requirements: Competency models must be developed at an appropriate level of granularity—too large a grain size yields less specific evidence, too fine a grain size increases complexity and resources
constraints: The framework must answer what attributes are to be measured and how they are scored, per the chapter's framing
target_learners: Learners in any assessment context from classroom quizzes to simulations
target_learning_goals: Valid, reliable inference of learner competency states to support diagnosis and instruction
examples: The chapter's Oblivion example instantiates ECD with a creative problem solving competency model, novelty/efficiency indicators, and a Bayes net
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25

article_title: Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes
citation: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884
title: Modern expectancy-value theory: multidimensional task value with four components
description: Modern EVT posits that achievement-related performance and choices are most directly influenced by expectancies of success and the subjective value of academic tasks. Task value is multidimensional: "Intrinsic value refers to the extent to which the person gains enjoyment from performing an activity", alongside attainment value (importance and identity relevance), utility value (usefulness), and cost (effort demands, lost alternatives, negative experiences). The study operationalizes these four components via ten facets and tests their unique and interactive prediction of outcomes.
requirements: Value components are measured as latent constructs with multiple facets per component, requiring sufficiently reliable multi-item scales
constraints: Cost is described as the least-studied component of task value
Expectancies of success and academic self-concept are not empirically separable, so self-concept is used as the expectancy measure
target_learners: secondary school students (German ninth-grade academic-track students)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement, effort, and behavioral engagement as outcomes of motivation
examples: The study measured the four components with 37 items covering 10 facets in 1,868 ninth-graders

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Evidence base of 49 randomized clinical trials evaluating 50 universal self-regulation interventions with 23,098 participants aged 2 to 17 years.
description: The review's evidence base comprises 49 studies reporting 50 interventions meeting all eligibility criteria, including "a total of 23,098 participants, a mean of 462 participants per study." Records were published over a span of 4 decades (1977-2017). On quality assessment using the Effective Public Health Practice Project Quality Assessment Tool, 3 studies were rated as high quality, 38 as moderate, and 8 as poor. The most common reason for downgrading was lack of blinding of participants (46 studies, 93.8%). Participants were predominantly in primary/elementary school (13,403, 58.0%) and preschool (6,566, 28.4%), with 84.8% in the United States and 34.3% low income.
requirements: Studies had to report cluster randomized trials or randomized clinical trials, evaluate universal interventions, include outcomes associated with self-regulation skills, and be published in a peer-reviewed journal with full text available in English
constraints: The review was limited to published literature in the English language and may have missed unpublished work and studies in other languages; generalizability may be affected by the substantial number of studies conducted in the United States
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 2 to 17 years (median 6.0 years) across preschool, primary, middle, and high school settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation outcomes measured via validated tools including the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function, Head Toes Knees Shoulders task, and Flanker tasks

article_title: Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension Among At-Risk Readers
citation: Miller Amanda C., Fuchs Douglas, Fuchs Lynn S., Compton Donald L., Kearns Devin, Zhang Wenjuan, Yen Loulee, Patton Samuel, Kirchner Danielle. (2014). Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension among At-Risk Readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 7(3), 232-249. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2014.906691
title: Evaluate at-risk students' behavioral attention and add explicit attention-maintaining procedures when implementing intensive reading intervention
description: The article recommends that because teacher-rated attention uniquely predicts at-risk readers' word reading growth, interventionists should assess behavioral attention and consider embedding procedures to sustain it during instruction. It states that "the behavioral attention of at-risk students should be evaluated, and that interventionists and classroom teachers consider the addition of explicit procedures to maintain student attention." The recommendation is grounded in the study's path-analysis findings and prior evidence that attention is malleable.
requirements: Behavioral attention of at-risk students should be evaluated before or during intensive reading intervention
constraints: Prior evidence cited (Dion et al., 2011) suggests decreasing the adverse effect of inattention may not be easy: inattentive students showed little reading gain even with the Good Behavior Game added to PALS
target_learners: at-risk first-grade readers with low behavioral attention
target_learning_goals: word reading growth
reading comprehension
examples: The study itself did not manipulate attention; the authors call for future studies to develop and empirically test attention-boosting procedures embedded in reading interventions and classroom instruction

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Event-centered analysis as an alternative to variable-centered methodologies for CSCL processes unfolding over time
description: Peter Reimann proposes an event-centered approach as an alternative to conventional variable-centered methodologies for analyzing processes in CSCL settings. The editorial reports that "tracking events can be more responsive to changing circumstances than plotting values of presumably fixed variables," and that event-centered analysis can account for richer causality and narrative reporting. It reflects on multiple analytic methods in CSCL at a fundamental conceptual level.
requirements: Analytic methods must handle processes that unfold over extended periods of time in CSCL settings
constraints: The editorial notes the approach does not clearly distinguish conversation analysis, uptake diagrams, and thick descriptions by participants' perspective on semantics, temporality, or interaction
target_learners: CSCL researchers and analysts of collaborative learning data
target_learning_goals: Analyzing collaborative learning processes over time

citation: Meg Farrell, Monika Martin, Ricardo Böheim, Alexander Renkl, Werner Rieß, Karen D. Könings, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer, Tina Seidel. (2024). Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Evidence-based scripted video cases of small-group tutoring as novice learning material
description: The article describes its scripted videos as representations of practice for approximating the core practice of small-group instruction. "The development and production process we undertook for the creation of our scripted video learning materials (of the present study and associated project studies) followed an evidence-based approach according to Dieker and coleagues (2009), Kim and colleagues (2006), and Piwowar and colleagues (2018)". Scripts were built from mock-up lessons on the circulatory system, with editing that reduces extraneous information and makes target learning material salient, lowering cognitive demand for novices.
requirements: scripted videos developed according to evidence-based guidelines so they are "particularly useful for novices"
constraints: mock-up scripts had to "represent a balance of the target learning content in each scenario in a concise way, but also retain sufficient authenticity"
target_learning_goals: noticing and reasoning about tutoring strategies for small group instruction
examples: A preliminary project study rated the videos' authenticity at M = 3.00, SD = 0.46 on a 4-point scale.

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Evolutionary psychological taxonomy distinguishing exploration, object play, and tool use by physiological features and developmental timing
description: The evolutionary psychology perspective distinguishes object-oriented behaviors "based on their difference in physiological features, developmental histories, and developmental consequences". Exploration is defined by elevated heart rate, low distractibility, and negative/flat affect; object play by lower heart rate, high distractibility, and positive affect, with purposelessness, repetition, segmentation, sequential variation, and exaggeration as features; tool use is the instrumental use of an object toward a goal. Construction is a later, accommodative behavior concerned with the end product, occurring between 3 and 5 years.
requirements: Distinguishing the behaviors relies on observable physiological markers such as heart rate, distractibility, and affect
constraints: The age range for tool use is described as less rigid, developing somewhere during infancy-childhood
target_learning_goals: tool use
social cognition
adaptation
examples: In the bottle example, squeezing the nipple is exploration, presenting the bottle for pretend drinking is object play, and drinking from the bottle is tool use.

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Analogy between human cognition and evolution by natural selection as natural information-processing systems underpinning cognitive load theory
description: The article proposes that the information processing characteristics of human cognitive architecture and evolution by natural selection are analogous, with both constituting natural information-processing systems. Problem solving corresponds to random generation and test analogous to random mutation, learning from others corresponds to reproduction, working memory corresponds to the epigenetic system, and long-term memory corresponds to the unlimited genetic code. The author argues this analogy strengthens the theory's base and underpins the emphasis on building stores of information in long-term memory as the major aim of instruction.
requirements: The analogy's validity is conditional: the article states that if the analogy is valid, the factors relevant to instructional design can be refined
constraints: The article presents this as an analogy whose validity is asserted rather than experimentally tested in this essay
target_learning_goals: building stores of relevant information in long-term memory for later use
examples: The article maps each cognitive component onto an evolutionary counterpart, e.g. retrieval from long-term memory to govern action is analogous to the epigenetic system using environmental cues to turn genes on or off
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial
citation: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4
title: EVCT-CLT model linking motivational beliefs directly to cognitive load
description: Feldon et al. (2019) propose an Expectancy-Value-Cost Theory-Cognitive Load Theory model in which "motivational beliefs and changes therein can result directly from cognitive load and manipulations thereof." Integrating the two research traditions combines EVCT's perspective on motivation and self-regulation with CLT's tradition of carefully designed randomized controlled experiments, and the authors suggest designs for new experiments and measurement approaches.
requirements: New experiments on relations between motivation, self-regulation, and cognitive load, and measurement of these constructs
constraints: Much existing research on links among EVCT constructs relied on correlational research methodologies
target_learning_goals: motivation and self-regulation in learning
examples: Feldon and colleagues provide suggestions for the design of new experiments on relations between motivation, self-regulation, and cognitive load

article_title: Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning
citation: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4
title: Geary's evolutionary approach to knowledge: primary versus secondary knowledge
description: The article organizes its predictions around Geary's evolutionary approach, in which "humans are able to easily acquire primary knowledge and, with more efforts, secondary knowledge". Primary knowledge is evolutionarily salient content such as rules about food and animals, while secondary knowledge is culturally invented content such as formal mathematics and grammar. The authors use this distinction to predict that framing formal logical problems in primary contexts should raise efficiency, motivation and engagement, and propose the approach as "a framework for developing a way to present new content that is cost-efficient in keeping learners motivated".
requirements: Learning tasks must distinguish content that is evolutionarily salient (primary) from culturally invented formal content (secondary)
target_learning_goals: formal logical reasoning (syllogisms)
examples: Syllogism training materials framed as rules about invented food and animals (primary) versus fictitious mathematics and grammar rules (secondary)
key_sources: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4

article_title: Children’s Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education
citation: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z
title: Four evolved learning mechanisms make humans highly educable
description: The article organizes human educability around four evolved mechanisms: "skeletal perceptual and cognitive mechanisms that get fleshed out over the course of development, mainly through play"; plasticity greatest early but persisting into adulthood; remarkable social-learning capabilities; and dispositions toward exploration and play. It uses this framework to explain how children are prepared to learn and why modern schooling sometimes conflicts with it.
requirements: Applies to understanding how children learn across development, with mechanisms fleshed out through experience rather than fully specified at birth
constraints: Framed as an evolutionary account of children's learning rather than a tested instructional intervention
target_learners: children from early childhood through adolescence
target_learning_goals: understanding how children's evolved learning mechanisms support acquisition of knowledge and skills
key_sources: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z

article_title: Children’s Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education
citation: Bjorklund, D.F. (2022). Children's Evolved Learning Abilities and Their Implications for Education. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 2243-2273. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09688-z
title: Evolutionary mismatches explain conflicts between evolved learning mechanisms and modern schooling
description: The article defines evolutionary mismatches as "conflicts between psychological mechanisms evolved in ancient environments and their utility in modern ones," examined "specifically with respect to modern educational systems." This account explains why some school practices fit poorly with children's evolved learning abilities and motivates the article's recommendations for aligning education with those abilities.
requirements: Requires identifying which psychological mechanisms were shaped in ancestral environments and how modern educational settings differ from them
constraints: Applied in the article specifically to modern educational systems
target_learning_goals: diagnosing why schooling can conflict with children's evolved ways of learning

article_title: An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks
citation: Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2011). An Evolutionary Upgrade of Cognitive Load Theory: Using the Human Motor System and Collaboration to Support the Learning of Complex Cognitive Tasks. Educ Psychol Rev (2012) 24:27–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9179-2
title: Evolutionary upgrade of cognitive load theory: biologically primary vs. biologically secondary knowledge
description: The article amends cognitive load theory using Geary's evolutionary account. Working memory limitations are critical only for biologically secondary information — culturally important knowledge we have not evolved to acquire, such as reading and mathematics — while biologically primary information, which the brain has evolved to process, is acquired "without a discernible working memory load". The paper uses this distinction to reinterpret cognitive load effects and to ask whether primary systems can facilitate secondary learning.
requirements: The distinction applies to instructional design for biologically secondary subject matter taught in educational and training contexts
constraints: It may not always be obvious in the absence of an evolutionary history into which category a particular skill should be placed; many skills may combine primary and secondary knowledge, forming more a continuum than a dichotomy
target_learners: school and university students acquiring biologically secondary subject matter
target_learning_goals: acquisition of culturally important, explicitly taught knowledge such as reading and mathematics
examples: Speaking and face recognition are given as primary knowledge acquired unconsciously and effortlessly; reading and mathematics as secondary knowledge requiring explicit instruction and extrinsic motivation

article_title: Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write
citation: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X
title: Evaluate spelling and graphomotor skill together: low word frequency with difficult letters can mimic graphomotor difficulty
description: Because orthographic and graphomotor constraints interact in beginning writers, assessing them separately can mislead teachers. The article states that this interaction "calls into question the relevance of evaluating spelling and graphomotor processes separately". If the word to be written is infrequent and contains difficult letters, handwriting performance may drop and the teacher could wrongly interpret this as a graphomotor difficulty. The principle therefore asks evaluators to consider word orthographic properties when judging handwriting quality, and letter difficulty when judging spelling.
requirements: Evaluation tasks must be designed so that the orthographic properties of the words (frequency, graphemic complexity) and the motor difficulty of their letters are known or controlled
constraints: The article notes the main limit is the reduced number of items used, due to the very controlled material, and further studies are necessary to confirm the combined effect
target_learners: primary school students, especially beginning writers in Grade 1
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of handwriting quality and spelling proficiency
examples: The article warns that handwriting performance on infrequent words containing difficult letters could be wrongly interpreted as a graphomotor difficulty, which might explain some handwriting difficulties observed in children with reading disorders
key_sources: Danna, J., Longcamp, M., Nalborczyk, L., Velay, J.-L., Commengé, C., & Jover, M. (2021). Interaction between orthographic and graphomotor constraints in learning to write. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3596-880X

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--VII.
citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey
title: Evaluate intelligence tests by their efficiency at the concrete practical problem they were built for, not by intrinsic psychometric appeal
description: Pressey proposes a problem-driven standard for test construction and evaluation: a test is satisfactory only insofar as it deals efficiently with the practical problem that motivated it, such as surveying a school system to find children who should be placed in special classes. As he puts it, "there is no value in measuring intelligence simply for the sake of measuring it; the tests are given in an effort to deal with some practical problem."
requirements: The practical problem the test is meant to solve must be specified before the test is built and evaluated
constraints: Pressey frames this for prognosis and class-placement problems in schools, not as a general theory of what intelligence is
target_learners: school children being screened for special or regular classes
target_learning_goals: appropriate educational placement and prognosis of school capacity
examples: For placing children in special classes, he recommends building an examination not involving matters taught specifically in school, but as much like school work as possible in other respects
key_sources: Pressey, S. L. (1920). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Intelligence+and+Its+Measurement+Pressey

article_title: The neurocognitive mechanism underlying math avoidance among math anxious people
citation: Jie Liu, Zhifeng Li, Jiawang Yang, Hao He & Fang Cui. (2025). The neurocognitive mechanism underlying math avoidance among math anxious people. npj Science of Learning 10:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00343-0
title: Expected Value of Control (EVC) account of math avoidance in high math anxiety
description: The article frames its neural findings with Expected Value of Control theory: people "integrate information about the expected reward and efﬁcacy of task performance to determine the expected value of control, and then adjust their control allocation (i.e., mental effort) accordingly". In the approach-avoid task, participants weighed their effectiveness at solving arithmetic problems against the rewards on offer. The authors propose that HMA individuals, lacking self-efficacy in mathematical ability, generate a lower expected value of cognitive control and so allocate less mental effort to accepting problems, aligning with the observed difficulty-driven avoidance.
requirements: Requires a context in which learners weigh expected reward and perceived efficacy of task performance before deciding whether to engage cognitive effort
constraints: The authors' application to HMA is an interpretation of the observed findings, not a direct test of EVC theory
examples: In the study's task, participants considered their effectiveness in solving arithmetic problems and the corresponding rewards to decide whether to accept or reject challenges
key_sources: Jie Liu, Zhifeng Li, Jiawang Yang, Hao He & Fang Cui. (2025). The neurocognitive mechanism underlying math avoidance among math anxious people. npj Science of Learning 10:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00343-0

article_title: Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation
citation: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9
title: Schedule motor practice sessions in the evening, close to sleep, when consolidation is the goal
description: This principle holds that the timing of practice, not just its amount, determines how well a newly trained motor skill survives to the next day. The article reports that "the timing of practice is an important factor for motor consolidation, which is better after training in the evening than in the morning". Because acquisition did not differ across times of day but consolidation did, scheduling near the night of sleep is the lever trainers control. The authors state the finding "may help in planning effective interventions in sports and rehabilitation".
requirements: A training session ending in the evening so that a night of sleep follows soon after practice
constraints: The conclusion applies primarily to individuals with an intermediate chronotype, as the majority of participants belonged to this type
New investigations are necessary to generalize the results and understand the underlying neural mechanisms
target_learners: Adults learning fine motor skills, e.g., athletes and patients in rehabilitation
target_learning_goals: Motor skill consolidation and retention between practice sessions
examples: Participants who trained at 8 p.m. improved skill 24 h later (12/12 increased), while morning-trained participants deteriorated (9/12 decreased)

article_title: Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance
citation: Ackermann, H., Henke, A., Chevalère, J., Yun, H. S., Hafner, V. V., Pinkwart, N., & Lazarides, R. (2025). Physical embodiment and anthropomorphism of AI tutors and their role in student enjoyment and performance. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00293-z
title: Evaluate anthropomorphism of pedagogical agents by subdimension and balance human-like traits against potential negative perceptions
description: The article recommends that designers of robotic tutors not treat anthropomorphism as uniformly beneficial. As the authors put it, "our results suggest that high anthropomorphism– negative as well as positive human-like traits– might not always be beneﬁcial for learning and should be evaluated with respect to different subdimensions." Perceived sociability was linked to lower task performance and perceived disturbance to lower enjoyment, so designs should balance human-like traits with mitigating negative perceptions, considering learners' individual prerequisites such as language proficiency.
requirements: Assessment instruments that distinguish subdimensions of anthropomorphism (e.g., sociability, animacy, agency, disturbance) rather than a single anthropomorphism score
constraints: Findings are based on a specific sample and experimental setup with 56 students and a 1-hour interaction; the authors call for validation with diverse participant groups and longer interactions
target_learners: school-aged students learning with AI-based tutoring systems and social robots
target_learning_goals: maintaining on-task enjoyment and task performance when learning with robotic tutor agents
examples: The study measured sociability, animacy, agency, and disturbance separately with the HRIES and found only sociability (negatively predicting performance) and disturbance (negatively predicting novelty-phase enjoyment) significant

article_title: Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality
citation: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6
title: Event segmentation theory: hierarchical perceptual and conceptual boundaries structure episodic memory, with top-down processes dominating bottom-up ones
description: Event segmentation theory holds that episodic memory is structured by event boundaries arising from contextual shifts. "Changes in motion, location, color, and sound result in perceptual boundaries", delineating lower-level sub-events, while "Changes in expectations, goals, and task sets formconceptualboundaries" delineating higher-level events; together they shape a hierarchical temporal structure. Contextual shifts disrupt predictions, generate prediction errors, and establish boundaries that segment continuous experience into event models, which serve as anchors for temporal order memory. The article applies the theory to predict and interpret differential effects of mission versus spatial boundaries in a VR task.
requirements: Contextual shifts during encoding that can be distinguished into perceptual and conceptual types
A memory measure sensitive to whether items fall within or across event models, such as recency discrimination
constraints: The relative prominence of one boundary type over the other may shift dynamically depending on the nature of the ongoing activity and individual goals
target_learners: healthy adult volunteers in episodic memory experiments
target_learning_goals: temporal order memory for sequentially encountered events
examples: In the VR salesperson task, mission boundaries defined by customer identity impaired sequence memory accuracy while booth-defined spatial boundaries did not
key_sources: Yue Li, Mikael Johansson & Andrey R. Nikolaev. (2025). Hierarchical event segmentation of episodic memory in virtual reality. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00321-6

article_title: Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER)
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7
title: The EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER) as a framework for evaluating EdTech evidence
description: EVER is a simple guide proposed by the authors to evaluate the evidence base of existing EdTech solutions and to help companies grow their products' evidence base. It is a matrix crossing evaluation approaches (conceptual, qualitative, quantitative, validation) with quality assurance aspects, with each cell rated. The authors state it "can be used as a prompt for reflection when evaluating the evidence portfolio of diverse EdTech products, processes and initiatives" and is best used as part of formative evaluations.
requirements: Criteria for assigning scores differ across evaluation method types, so users must apply type-appropriate criteria
constraints: EVER is best used as part of formative evaluations; it is not intended to determine good or bad solutions
It should be supplemented with other frameworks targeting cost-effectiveness, data privacy and teachers' usability evaluations
target_learning_goals: Literacy and math foundational skills
Behaviour change
Assessment combined with intervention
examples: Applied to EdTech for assessment, intervention or edutainment in K-12 education, at lifecycle stages from pre-company accelerator stage to mature companies seeking funding

article_title: Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER)
citation: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7
title: Four quality assurance aspects for judging EdTech evidence: methodological quality, outcome strength, generalizability, ethics and transparency
description: EVER organizes evidence quality along four aspects. Methodological quality asks whether methods are appropriately executed, described and justified. Outcome strength concerns sizable impact or predictive value, quantified via effect size or sensitivity/specificity. Generalizability is the extension of findings from one sample to the target population, requiring representativeness. Ethics and transparency ensure ethical design, users' well-being, culturally-responsive approaches and transparent data use.
requirements: Each criterion's strength is rated on a 0–5 point-scale for each cell, including cells where the company has no activity
constraints: A larger sample typically comes with higher generalizability but still needs to match the target population in demographic characteristics, socio-cultural values, skills and abilities
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether EdTech works, for whom, and ethically
examples: The aspects answer stakeholder questions such as whether the tool works for my students, how much of an effect it has, and whether users know which personal data are collected
key_sources: Natalia Kucirkova, Garvin Brod and Nadine Gaab. (2023). Applying the science of learning to EdTech evidence evaluations using the EdTech Evidence Evaluation Routine (EVER). npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00186-7

title: EVER's Table 1 matrix of four evaluation approaches by four quality assurance aspects
description: Table 1 outlines the evidence base and evaluation approaches employed to test an EdTech product (rows: conceptual, qualitative, quantitative, validation) crossed with quality assurance aspects (columns: methodological quality, outcome strength/predictive value, generalizability, ethics and transparency), each cell marked for rating. The authors note criteria can differ by method type, e.g. methodological quality criteria for conceptual studies can differ from generalisability criteria in quantitative or qualitative studies.

examples: The matrix is applied in conjunction with local quality assurance assessments at district or school level and by EdTech developers in iterative product development
