citation: Chih-Pu Dai · Fengfeng Ke. (2026). Model-based support for teaching practice and self-efficacy in artificial intelligence-enhanced virtual reality teaching simulation. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10592-4
title: EVETeach: an AI-enhanced VR teaching simulation with a generative AI virtual student agent
description: EVETeach (Enactive Virtual Environment for teaching) is a VR simulation-based learning environment built on the open-source OpenSimulator platform. Its core element is an AI-powered virtual student agent, called Evelyn, created by refining a generative AI model with a localized dataset of ambitious teaching classroom videos and TIMSS video clips, so that the agent "can question, respond and interact with the preservice teachers in an authentic and domain-specific manner."

Classroom discussion facilitation

article_title: Academic, social, and cultural learning in the French #bac2018 Twitter hashtag
citation: Greenhalgh, S. P., Nnagboro, C., Kaufmann, R., & Gretter, S. (2021). Academic, social, and cultural learning in the French #bac2018 Twitter hashtag. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 1835-1851. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10015-6
title: Evaluate educational social media against broad learning manifestations, not academic performance alone
description: This principle holds that judgments about whether a platform like Twitter contributes to learning should account for social and cultural practices as well as academic outcomes. The article argues that narrow, performance-based evaluation produces unwarranted skepticism, since #bac2018 practices "were associated with not only academic learning but also social and cultural practices". It recommends, in effect, widening the lens used to assess learning in digital contexts.
requirements: Evaluation criteria that can capture social and cultural practices, not only test scores or grades
constraints: The article demonstrates this with one hashtag around one exam period; generalization to other platforms and events is not tested
target_learners: Educators and researchers evaluating social media for learning
target_learning_goals: Fair assessment of learning occurring in social media contexts
examples: The authors documented eight tweeting practices in #bac2018 and read them as academic, social, and cultural learning rather than scoring them against exam performance

article_title: Supporting learners’ experiment design
citation: Siswa van Riesen, Hannie Gijlers, Anjo Anjewierden, Ton de Jong. (2018). Supporting learners' experiment design. Education Tech Research Dev (2018) 66:475–491. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9568-4
title: Evaluate learners' prior knowledge when introducing scaffolds for experiment design, because scaffold effectiveness depends on learner characteristics
description: The article's results show "there's no one-size-fits-all approach that applies to learners' guidance regarding experiment design, and that prior knowledge should be evaluated when introducing scaffolds." The EDT significantly helped low prior knowledge learners but showed no overall advantage, indicating the effect of scaffolding "is very much influenced by the context and can be different per situation." The authors argue the Scaffolding Design Framework should be adapted to stress the importance of context, learner characteristics, domain characteristics, and place in the curriculum.
requirements: Assessment of learners' prior knowledge before deciding on the level of guidance to provide
constraints: The finding was demonstrated in one domain (Archimedes' principle) with pre-university track secondary students; the article states the effect of scaffolding can differ per situation
target_learners: secondary school science learners with varying prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: designing informative experiments
conceptual knowledge gain in inquiry learning
examples: In the study, only low prior knowledge learners (63 of 86) benefited significantly from the EDT, while the full-sample comparison showed no condition differences.

citation: Samuel O. King and Carol Robinson. (2008). 'Pretty Lights' and Maths! Increasing student engagement and enhancing learning through the use of electronic voting systems. Mathematics Education Centre, Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Use EVS primarily in formative-assessment mode so instant feedback empowers students and informs lecturers' pedagogical adjustments
description: The paper argues the value of EVS lies in formative feedback: it is instant, acts as "a barometer for personal understanding of study", lets students gauge the class, and gives staff knowledge of what needs correcting or reinforcing. The authors state that "The formative feedback that the use of EVS engenders is pivotal in the learning process", enabling lecturers lacking a week-by-week sense of student assimilation to make pedagogical changes addressing gaps.

constraints: Feedback's benefit depends on lecturers having and using a means of gauging student assimilation; without it, necessary pedagogical changes cannot be made

identification of problem areas
lecturer awareness of class-wide misconceptions

title: Future simulation-versus-patient-based evaluations should also measure clinical and patient-based outcomes
description: This principle states that comparisons of simulation-based education with patient-based clinical teaching should extend beyond student assessments to clinical and patient outcomes, because the review found "No studies assessed patient‐based clinical outcomes, patient acceptability of nursing care given or staff resource time for teaching of the students." examples: The review's included studies used exams, OSCEs, knowledge tests, externally rated performance scores and clinical placement grades as outcome measures

citation: Somayeh Nilforoushan. (2012). The Effect of Teaching Vocabulary through Semantic Mapping on EFL Learners' Awareness of the Affective Dimensions of Deep Vocabulary Knowledge. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p164
title: Deep vocabulary knowledge includes the affective dimensions of evaluation and potency
description: Drawing on Osgood, May and Miron (1975) and Heise (2002), the article treats deep vocabulary knowledge — how well a person knows a word, as opposed to how many words are known — as involving evaluation, potency, and activity of vocabularies. The "Evaluative dimension of vocabulary knowledge refers to how good or bad something is", while the potency dimension "refers to an entity`s impact in terms of being big verses little, powerful verses powerless". The study operationalizes these dimensions with potent/positive, potent/negative, non-potent/positive, and non-potent/negative adjectives and interpersonal verbs.
requirements: Assessment requires adjective and verb classifications for evaluation and potency, taken from Carrigon tables of evaluating and potency (2002)
constraints: The study examined only the evaluation and potency dimensions, not the activity dimension named by Osgood, May and Miron
target_learning_goals: awareness of the evaluative and potency dimensions of word meaning in interpersonal language use
examples: The awareness posttest paired verbs with proper names in sentences such as "John hit Ted", and students chose adjectives that best described each noun.

title: Admissions processes should evaluate undergraduate course withdrawal patterns alongside GPA when identifying students at risk of academic difficulty.
description: The article recommends that admissions committees attend to course withdrawal histories, a metric the authors say "have received less attention from admissions committees," because withdrawals predicted both probation and attrition while GPA predicted only probation. The authors suggest that higher-risk students may withdraw from pre-PA courses to protect their GPAs, meaning GPA alone may mask risk that withdrawal counts reveal. examples: The program used these findings to inform its admissions process by identifying students who may need more academic support at the start of PA training.

title: Evocative gene–environment correlation via the school social environment
description: The article extends evocative rGE theory—children's genetically influenced traits eliciting responses from others—to the school context, proposing that education-linked genetic propensities evoke differential teacher responses (lower conflict, more positivity), which in turn partially transmit genetic effects to educational outcomes. Because "teachers and children are genetically unrelated, associations between child education polygenic scores (PGSedu) and the student–teacher relationship cannot reflect shared genetics, reducing a key source of confounding."
requirements: Genetically unrelated informants (teachers) to separate child genetic effects from shared genetic confounding
constraints: Indirect parental genetic effects and SES-linked environmental pathways may still contribute; PGSedu is a pleiotropic aggregate, not a narrow academic-ability measure
target_learning_goals: educational performance in reading and mathematics
examples: The study tested this account with preregistered SEMs in 63,032 MoBa children, finding conflict and teacher-response positivity, but not closeness, carried the evoked signal

article_title: Non-cognitive skills mediate education-related polygenic score associations with academic achievement across development.
citation: Quan Zhou, Liao Wangjingyi, Allegrini Andrea G., Rimfeld Kaili, Wertz Jasmin, Morris Tim T., Raffington Laurel, Plomin Robert, Malanchini Margherita. (2026). Non-cognitive skills mediate education-related polygenic score associations with academic achievement across development. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72838-2
title: Evocative/active gene-environment correlation framework: children actively select environments aligned with their non-cognitive characteristics, translating genetic dispositions into academic outcomes
description: The article frames its findings within transactional models of human development rooted in evocative/active gene-environment correlation, proposing that "children actively seek out different environmental experiences on the basis of their non-cognitive characteristics (e.g., interests, preferences, and aptitudes), and in turn, these will lead to different learning outcomes". This framework explains why non-cognitive skills mediate genetic associations with achievement: as children develop greater self-awareness and autonomy, they shape their environmental contexts in ways that cultivate these skills and foster academic performance. The within-family findings, where mediation persists beyond shared family factors, support this individual-specific selection mechanism.
requirements: Longitudinal data on non-cognitive skills and academic achievement across multiple raters and timepoints
constraints: Mediation effects are modest in magnitude and the study cannot exclude potential genetic confounding in mediation analyses
target_learners: children and adolescents in compulsory education (ages 7-16)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in English, mathematics, and science

Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 67(2), 158–170. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.70025
title: Evocative gene–environment correlation as a mechanism amplifying genetic influence on educational outcomes
description: The article tests the framework that increasing heritability of cognitive and educational abilities with age partly reflects evocative gene–environment correlation (rGE), in which "individuals' genetically influenced characteristics systematically evoke differences in their environment, potentially mediating genetic effects". In this study, children's education polygenic scores were hypothesized to evoke differences in maternal parenting and language, which in turn mediate genetic effects on educational performance. The framework explains how environmental effects correlated with genetic differences can be obscured by global heritability estimates.
requirements: Large genetically informative samples (e.g., parent–offspring trios with parental genotypes) are needed to separate evocative from passive gene–environment correlation.
constraints: Polygenic scores currently explain a fraction of heritability (PGSedu explained 11% of variance in parent educational attainment in the sample), so effects may be underestimated and null effects may be false negatives.
The study analyzed biologically related parent–offspring, making it difficult to separate genetic from shared environmental effects.
target_learners: Children in early childhood (age 5) and early primary school (ages 6–8)
target_learning_goals: Educational performance (reading and arithmetic)
Early language development
examples: The study tested three preregistered hypotheses in 83,627 MoBa parent–offspring trios using structural equation models controlling for both parents' PGSedu.

title: Event-level aggregation of gaze parameters using participant-defined event segmentation as the unit of analysis
description: The article proposes analyzing gaze metrics (fixation duration, saccade amplitude, pupil diameter) aggregated within participant-defined events rather than across heterogeneous timelines, drawing on Event Segmentation Theory, which "posits that we engage in segmentation in a hierarchical manner" into coarse and fine events. title: Expectancy-Value Theory as a framework for test-taking motivation and feedback use
description: The article uses Expectancy Value Theory as its conceptual framework for test-taking motivation, stating that "motivation for a task depends on expectancies of success, and perceived value given to the task". Test-taking effort is treated as the main element of test-taking motivation, the direct outcome of expectancy and value. The study's interviews operationalised value as experienced utility value (usefulness) and attainment value (importance) of the progress test, linking value to test-taking effort and thence to feedback consultation.

title: Evaluate available human and material resources before implementing a trauma team training program
description: The review infers a matching principle for trauma team training adoption: planners should first assess local capacity. It states that 'an evaluation of available human and material resources should be performed before implementing any training program', and that choosing the appropriate training program and education delivery method could be key to achieving improved patient care and outcomes. This follows its account of curricula that fit constrained settings, such as PTC and RTTDC.

constraints: Established curricula like ATLS have proved difficult in low and middle-income countries due to training costs and scarcity of trainers, and require readily available high-tech equipment such as CT scanners and bedside ultrasound

emergency staff in low and middle-income countries and rural non-trauma hospitals
target_learning_goals: coordinated assessment and management of severe, life-threatening injuries
selection of a training program appropriate to local trauma care delivery
examples: The review describes the Primary Trauma Care course as a free, WHO-endorsed adaptation of ATLS basic principles designed to be self-perpetuating and sustainable in low-resource settings, and RTTDC as training small rural teams to identify and transfer patients within the first 15 min of presentation.

citation: Cano García, E., Halbaut Bellowa, L., Martins Gironelli, L., & Lluch Molins, L. (2024). Online peer assessment in Galenic Pharmacy: enhancing evaluative judgement in higher education. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2409487
title: Evaluative judgement as the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others
description: The article defines evaluative judgement as "the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others" [27, p. 472]. It involves comparing one's own or others' work with pre-established standards, rubric indicators or exemplary work, applying quality criteria and justifying assessments. The authors treat it as a cross-curricular competency linked to 'learning to learn' that enables students to judge quality without depending on external approval, stimulating autonomy and reflective thinking. Peer and self-assessment processes are the strategies the article uses to develop it.
requirements: Opportunities for everyone to gain knowledge of the criteria, apply them, and obtain feedback on the quality of their work
constraints: Limiting factors include lack of competence trust, tensions in feedback communication, competition or lack of readiness for peer learning
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgement
critical judgement
learning to learn
